Unless my understanding of the subject is incorrect, if freshwater comes into contact with saltwater (such as rivers depositing into oceans), the freshwater sinks under the saltwater in a similar way to the interaction of water and oil.
When freshwater is mixed with saltwater, why does it not become less salty water?

If you are talking about why the oceans stay salty with rivers of freshwater emptying into them, the freshwater contains dissolved minerals that are left behind when the water evaporates out of the oceans:

http://water.usgs.gov/edu/whyoceansalty.html
Well there is brackish water too, a mix between fresh and salt water. A good example of this is Östersjön, the "ocean" located between Sweden and Finland.

If the two waters mix, then it will definitely be water of intermediate saltiness. There's actually a neat test that you can do to with a fish tank to see the changing salinity.

 

Fill the tank with fresh water.

Place a separator in the tank such that you split the water in half down the middle (the seal doesn't have to be perfect).

Mix some salt and blue food dye into one half of the tank, and just some yellow food dye in the other half.

Carefully take out the separator.

Watch the water stratify into the two layer as you originally described.

Now, put the separator back 3/4 of the way along the tank.

In the smaller part of the tank (the 1/4), mix together the water so that it's a nice green colour. (this is your mixed intermediate salty water).

Again, carefully lift out the separator.

Now you have fresh, salty, and mixed (yet still salty) waters
